The paper develops a two-fluid model (TFM) for heat transfer in dense non-Brownian suspensions.
The TFM includes separate mass, momentum, and energy conservation equations for the particle and fluid phases.
The particle phase stress tensor is modeled using rheological closures that capture the anisotropy due to shearing.
The paper proposes a shear-dependent inter-phase heat transfer coefficient 𝐾 = 𝐾 [1 + 𝛽𝜙(‖𝑺̇ ‖𝑑 /𝛼 )^𝑚], where 𝛽 = 0.2 and 𝑚 = 1 are calibrated parameters.
The 'thermo-rheological' migration force opposes the classical shear-induced migration and is oriented in the direction of the temperature gradient.
The TFM was calibrated against the heat pulse experiments of Metzger et al. for a Couette cell flow with 𝛾̇ = 10 s^-1.
The particle and fluid had identical thermal conductivity 𝑘 = 0.19 W/m-K, specific heat 𝐶 = 1260 J/kg-K, and density 𝜌 = 1180 kg/m^3.
During the 5s heating period, the inner cylinder was held at 298 K, while the outer cylinder was insulated. During cooling, an adiabatic BC was applied at the inner cylinder.
The paper showed that the geometric eccentricity of the Couette cell can be used to tune the thermal performance of the suspension flow.
Potential applications include geothermal energy recovery, hydraulic fracturing, hemodynamics, microfluidics, electronic cooling, and food processing.
Unlike the DFM and SBM, the TFM solves separate governing equations for the particle and fluid phases, without assuming thermal equilibrium.
The TFM can capture the inter-phase heat transfer and its coupling with particle migration, which is not possible in the DFM and SBM.
The paper identified a 'thermo-rheological' migration force that arises from the interplay between temperature-dependent fluid viscosity and anisotropic particle stresses.
The TFM was implemented in OpenFOAM using a finite volume method with a structured mesh and second-order discretization schemes.
A grid independence study was performed to determine the optimal number of mesh elements for accurate results.
